prompt: In the module example, why does modules/reports-bucket/main.tf omit the provider "aws" block that the Tier 2 root configuration had?
choices: Modules are not allowed to create any AWS resources at all.
A module doesn't configure its own provider; the calling root configuration supplies the provider, so the same module can be reused across different regions or accounts without modification.
The provider block is automatically copied into every module by terraform init.
Provider blocks are deprecated in modern Terraform and should never be used anywhere.

prompt: A root configuration calls the same module twice: module "team_reports" and module "billing_reports", each with a different bucket_name. What does terraform plan show?
choices: An error, because a module can only be called once per configuration.
Two independent resources, addressed as module.team_reports.aws_s3_bucket.reports and module.billing_reports.aws_s3_bucket.reports, each with its own real bucket name.
A single merged resource combining both bucket_name values.
Only the second module call takes effect; the first is silently overwritten.

prompt: Tier 2 named the single-laptop state risk: losing your local terraform.tfstate means Terraform might recreate or orphan real infrastructure. Concretely, how does an S3+DynamoDB remote backend fix this, beyond just moving the file off your laptop?
choices: It doesn't fix anything beyond storage location; locking is unrelated to the state-loss risk.
DynamoDB encrypts the state file so it can never be read even if leaked.

S3 gives durable, shared storage so no single machine is the only copy, and the DynamoDB lock table ensures only one apply can run against that state at a time, preventing the exact concurrent-write corruption Tier 2 described.
It replaces terraform.tfstate with a SQL database that enforces foreign key constraints on resource IDs.

prompt: You run terraform apply while a CI job already holds the DynamoDB state lock for the same backend key. What happens?
choices: Your apply proceeds normally; DynamoDB only logs a warning.
Your apply fails immediately with a state lock error naming who holds the lock, until that lock is released.
Terraform automatically queues your apply and runs it after the CI job finishes, with no error shown.
The state file is duplicated so both applies can proceed independently.

prompt: What does terraform.workspace provide, and how is it typically used?
choices: It's a manually-set string variable with no built-in meaning; you must declare it yourself in variables.tf.

It's a built-in reference to the currently selected workspace name (e.g. "dev" or "prod"), commonly used to look up per-environment values such as bucket_name from a local map, without needing a separate input variable for the environment name.
It's the local path to the current working directory, used only for logging.
It only exists inside Terraform Cloud and has no equivalent for local or S3-backed state.

prompt: You are in the dev workspace and run terraform destroy. What happens to the prod workspace's infrastructure, assuming both share the same backend?
choices: Both dev and prod resources are destroyed, since destroy always affects the whole backend.

Nothing - each workspace has its own isolated state (e.g. stored separately as env:/dev/... vs env:/prod/... under the same backend), so destroy in one workspace only affects that workspace's tracked resources.
Terraform prompts you to choose which workspace to destroy, but defaults to destroying all of them.
prod is destroyed instead of dev, because destroy always targets the last-created workspace.

prompt: In the Pulumi Python example, which Terraform concept does pulumi.export(...) most directly correspond to?
choices: A provider block.
A resource block.
A variable block.
An output block.

prompt: What is the concrete tradeoff the module draws between HCL-first Terraform and code-first Pulumi/CDK?
choices: HCL is strictly obsolete and every team should migrate to Pulumi or CDK immediately.
They are functionally identical in every respect, so the choice never matters.

HCL's limited expressiveness makes it harder to write complex logic but keeps configs boring and auditable; Pulumi/CDK use a real general-purpose language, giving full control flow and tooling at the cost of also being able to introduce real programming bugs into infrastructure code.
Pulumi and CDK cannot manage remote state at all, so they are only suitable for local experimentation.
